Here you will replace the two spheroids with `DebyeSphereCloud` subunits
built from PDB coordinates. You will use `PDBParser`, `AtomParameterProfile`,
and `AtomCloudBuilder`, then connect the same analytical chains to named
N- and C-terminal references.

**Keep:** the five-part topology and Gaussian linker and tails.
**Change:** the internal domain geometry, which is now fixed by coordinates.

::: {.callout-note title="Before you start"}
Complete [page 1](fit-linked-titin.qmd). For a smaller introduction to cloud
building, see [PDB cloud with an attached polymer](pdb-polymer.qmd).
:::

## Open the worked example

Run this page from `docs/tutorials` in a repository checkout, using the
[environment from page 1](fit-linked-titin.qmd#prepare-your-environment).
The setup loads the measured curve, saved fit values, and display helpers.
You can start a fresh kernel here; you do not need to run the previous page's fits.

{{< include _titin-setup.qmd >}}

The visible examples below run with this setup. Expand the calculation source
at the end if you want the complete fitting implementation.

## 1. Parse one domain

Select model 1 from the local four-model PDB extract. `PDBParser` returns
atoms that you can inspect before building a scattering subunit:

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
parse_options = pyseb.StructureParseOptions()
parse_options.model_number = 1
atoms = pyseb.PDBParser().parse_file(
    "data/1TIU-heavy-ensemble.pdb", parse_options)
alpha_carbons = [atom for atom in atoms if atom.atom_name == "CA"]
print("Heavy atoms:", len(atoms))
print("Terminal C-alpha serials:", alpha_carbons[0].serial, alpha_carbons[-1].serial)
```
The domain contains **688 heavy atoms**. Use the first and last C-alpha
atoms as attachment references. This gives `nterminus` and `cterminus` a
structural meaning while every heavy atom contributes to scattering.

## 2. Assign weights and name the attachment points

An `AtomParameterProfile` assigns a radius and amplitude weight to each element.
For this step, use zero-radius scatterers with constant weights proportional
to atomic number. Normalize their sum to 89 so the domain-to-chain weights
stay comparable to page 1.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
atomic_numbers = {"C": 6, "N": 7, "O": 8, "S": 16}
total_electrons = sum(atomic_numbers[atom.element] for atom in atoms)
profile = pyseb.AtomParameterProfile()
for element, electrons in atomic_numbers.items():
    profile.set_element(element, radius=0.0,
                        beta=89.0 * electrons / total_electrons)

build_options = pyseb.AtomCloudBuildOptions()
build_options.reference_atom_serials = {
    "nterminus": alpha_carbons[0].serial,
    "cterminus": alpha_carbons[-1].serial,
}
domain1 = pyseb.AtomCloudBuilder.build(atoms, profile, build_options)
domain2 = pyseb.AtomCloudBuilder.build(atoms, profile, build_options)
```
`AtomCloudBuilder.build` returns a subunit you can pass directly to
`World.Add` or `World.Link`. Its Debye sum retains all atom-pair distances.
We have introduced coordinate geometry; q-dependent atomic form factors and
solvent corrections come on the next page.

## 3. Connect the clouds using their named references

The graph-building API is the same as for analytical shapes. Replace the
spheroid type names with the cloud objects and use their terminal references:

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
world = pyseb.World("CoordinateTitinTutorial")
graph = world.Add(domain1, "domain1")
world.Link("GaussianPolymer", "ntail.end2", "domain1.nterminus")
world.Link("GaussianPolymer", "linker.end1", "domain1.cterminus")
world.Link(domain2, "domain2.nterminus", "linker.end2")
world.Link("GaussianPolymer", "ctail.end1", "domain2.cterminus")
_ = world.Add(graph, "titin")
```
Follow the central connection: `domain1.cterminus` → `linker.end1`, then
`linker.end2` → `domain2.nterminus`. The remaining domain termini carry the
tails. Each domain keeps its internal coordinates; pySEB averages relative
orientations and the analytical chain statistics.

## 4. Evaluate with the same parameter interface

Only four variables remain in the fit: linker size, terminal-chain size,
scale, and background. There are no adjustable domain semi-axes.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
linker_rg, tail_rg8, scale, background = results["fits"]["debye"]["x"]
parameters = {
    "Rg_linker": linker_rg, "beta_linker": 8.0,
    "Rg_ntail": tail_rg8 * np.sqrt(24.0 / 8.0), "beta_ntail": 24.0,
    "Rg_ctail": tail_rg8 * np.sqrt(7.0 / 8.0), "beta_ctail": 7.0,
}
form_factor = np.asarray(world.EvaluateFormFactor(
    "titin", parameters, q.tolist()))
compare_curves({
    "Constrained spheroids": curves["analytical_constrained"],
    "Coordinate domains": scale * form_factor + background,
})
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
fit_table("debye")
```
The saved fit gets **worse**: training reduced chi-squared rises from about
1.44 to **50.43**, and the linker reaches its **9 Å upper bound**. Fixing the
domain geometry removes one way for the optimizer to compensate. The remaining
chain and scattering assumptions do not describe the measurement well.

This is useful information from the model change. Keep the deposited domain
coordinates fixed and investigate the scattering assumptions next.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Coordinate and weight assumptions"}
The [1TIU](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1TIU) template has 89 residues and
differs from the measured construct by three substitutions: F21L, T42V, and
A78T, from template to construct. We use its coordinates without rebuilding
those side chains. The 24:89:8:89:7 weights are approximate residue-count
weights, rather than absolute electron-count contrasts.
:::

## 5. Inspect the attachments

Display the coordinate-based world with the same visualization API:

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
options = pyseb.USDExportOptions(pyseb.LengthUnit.Angstrom)
options.seed = 42
_ = pyseb.visualize(
    world, "titin", parameters, options, height=440,
    layouts=["random", "readable"],
)
```
Locate the linker endpoints and the two outer tails. The picture shows a
realization of the model, while the evaluated scattering averages over its
orientations and Gaussian chains.

**Try it:** vary the N-tail size without rebuilding either cloud:

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
trial_curves = {}
for factor in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5):
    trial = {**parameters, "Rg_ntail": factor * parameters["Rg_ntail"]}
    trial_p = np.asarray(world.EvaluateFormFactor("titin", trial, q.tolist()))
    trial_curves[f"N-tail Rg × {factor:g}; no refit"] = scale * trial_p + background
compare_curves(trial_curves)
```
This experiment changes one chain independently; the saved fit uses a shared
size scale for both tails. The cloud geometry and attachment references stay fixed.

## Continue

You can now turn parsed atoms into linked pySEB subunits. Next,
[configure atomic scattering and hydration](titin-hydration.qmd) to test the
weights assigned to those coordinates.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Complete calculation source: coordinate-domain fit"}

These are the complete calculation cells used by the sequence generator.
They run in sequence order across the four pages; fitting and export cells
are disabled during website rendering. The short examples above can be run
after this page's setup without regenerating the fits.

```{python}
#| tags: [titin-generation]
#| eval: false
pdb_path = data_directory / "1TIU-heavy-ensemble.pdb"
parse_options = pyseb.StructureParseOptions()
parse_options.model_number = 1
unscaled_atoms = pyseb.PDBParser().parse_file(str(pdb_path), parse_options)
terminal_atoms = [atom for atom in unscaled_atoms if atom.atom_name == "CA"]
print(f"Heavy-atom scatterers per I27 cloud: {len(unscaled_atoms)}")
print("Terminal C-alpha serials:", terminal_atoms[0].serial,
      terminal_atoms[-1].serial)
```

```{python}
#| tags: [titin-generation]
#| eval: false
def build_pdb_world():
    atoms = unscaled_atoms
    atomic_numbers = {"C": 6, "N": 7, "O": 8, "S": 16}
    total_electrons = sum(atomic_numbers[atom.element] for atom in atoms)
    profile = pyseb.AtomParameterProfile()
    for element, electrons in atomic_numbers.items():
        profile.set_element(element, radius=0.0,
                            beta=domain_beta * electrons / total_electrons)

    options = pyseb.AtomCloudBuildOptions()
    options.reference_atom_serials = {
        "nterminus": terminal_atoms[0].serial,
        "cterminus": terminal_atoms[-1].serial,
    }

    domain1 = pyseb.AtomCloudBuilder.build(atoms, profile, options)
    domain2 = pyseb.AtomCloudBuilder.build(atoms, profile, options)

    world = pyseb.World("TitinPDBClouds")
    graph = world.Add(domain1, "domain1")
    world.Link(
        "GaussianPolymer",
        "ntail.end2",
        "domain1.nterminus",
    )
    world.Link(
        "GaussianPolymer",
        "linker.end1",
        "domain1.cterminus",
    )
    world.Link(
        domain2,
        "domain2.nterminus",
        "linker.end2",
    )
    world.Link(
        "GaussianPolymer",
        "ctail.end1",
        "domain2.cterminus",
    )
    world.Add(graph, "titin")
    return world


pdb_world = build_pdb_world()


def pdb_curve(values, q_values):
    linker_rg, tail_rg8, scale, background = values
    parameters = construct_polymer_parameters(linker_rg, tail_rg8)
    form_factor = np.asarray(
        pdb_world.EvaluateFormFactor(
            "titin", parameters, q_values.tolist()
        )
    )
    return scale * form_factor + background


def pdb_residual(values):
    return (pdb_curve(values, fit_q) - fit_intensity) / fit_uncertainty


pdb_fit = least_squares(
    pdb_residual,
    x0=[5.0, 5.0, 0.033, 0.0002],
    bounds=(
        [linker_rg_bounds[0], 0.1, 0.0, 0.0],
        [linker_rg_bounds[1], 30.0, 1.0, 0.01],
    ),
    x_scale="jac",
)

pdb_names = [
    "linker Rg [A]",
    "terminal-chain Rg8 [A]",
    "scale",
    "background",
]
for name, value in zip(pdb_names, pdb_fit.x):
    print(f"{name:31s} = {value:.6g}")
print_derived_tail_radii(pdb_fit.x[1])
print(
    "reduced chi^2                 = "
    f"{reduced_chi_squared(pdb_fit.fun, pdb_fit.x.size):.3f}"
)
```

```{python}
#| tags: [titin-generation]
#| eval: false
show_structure(pdb_world, construct_polymer_parameters(*pdb_fit.x[:2]),
               "debye-domains")
compare_curves({
    "Constrained spheroids": spheroid_curve(spheroid_fit.x, q),
    "Heavy-atom Debye clouds": pdb_curve(pdb_fit.x, q),
})
```
